Simulation of what you would see if you fell into a Black Hole.
Genuine question. If a black hole has never been seen, how can anyone simulate or even describe what it would look like if you were pulled into one?

The description or simulation is based on the known behaviors of light. Since gravity bends light, and black holes "have a lot of gravity", they act like lenses; they bend light. The visual effects of bent light are pretty well understood, hence... a simulation is possible.

No one KNOWS what happens or what you would see... But based on the observations of light bending around black holes, observations of objects having mass also having more gravity, predictive equations that seem to fit and then have bits of them "proven" through experimentation... we have a pretty good idea of what light likely does around a black hole.

The thing about science is that everything we know might be wrong about everything... Because it's an iterative process. Without new information, science stops! You need new information to see how it fits into old theories or to form new ones. People who thought the sun revolved around the Earth weren't idiots. They just didn't have the same data we have. So, basically, we're making assumptions based on prior observations. "This thing is like this thing, so maybe it would do X the same way." That's uncomfortable and ridiculous to people who think science creates definitive answers, but it is exactly its malleability that makes it awesome. If we ever record the descent into a black hole and it looks nothing like this, some people will say "SCIENCE HAS FAILED US!" but Scientists will be super excited. Few things in science are as exciting as a totally unexpected outcome.

Here's a maybe decent visual of how gravity affects things... but it's not perfect.

Think of light as a particle (a photon!). Which means you can think of it as a rock. If you throw a rock past Earth, as you've probably seen from other videos or simulations of a comet or whatever, the rock won't go in a straight line, it will bend towards Earth. The more time the rock spends near the gravitational field of the Earth, the more its flight path will be altered by the Earth's gravity. Since light is so fast and would spend so little time near the Earth, it isn't effected by the gravitational field as much. So for something to significantly gravitationally alter the path of light, it has to be kind of a big deal. Anyway... Don't think of it as "bending" a bar or iron rod.
